transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2027-07-02 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~56 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Patel (Redwood SE), Samir Rao (CTO - LatticeWave), Nina Lopez (Head of MLOps), Ethan Park (Infra), Priya Desai (Product)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be noisy): LatticeWave looking to move critical inference workloads off of open cloud bursts into stable reserved capacity; strong concerns about noisy neighbors, encryption at rest, KMS/HSM, and the ability to handle periodic marketing spikes ~5x baseline for 1-2 hours. Redwood explained dedicated pools, warm-pools, pre-warm strategies, routing/fallback to hosted Redwood models, and proposed a pilot + benchmark.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you taking the time. Quick intros? I can start, I'm Maya, AE covering enterprise infra at Redwood. Jordan is our SE for dedicated and private deployments.
[00:12] Jordan (Redwood SE): Hi all, Jordan here — I'll be the technical lead on this topic.
[00:16] Samir (LatticeWave - CTO): Samir — I'm running infra and platform. We've been running a mix of self-hosted inference and hosted endpoints and trying to figure out next step for high critical paths.
[00:22] Nina (Head of MLOps): Nina here — responsible for model ops and rollout cadence.
[00:26] Ethan (Infra): Ethan, infra engineer.
[00:29] Priya (Product): Priya from product.
[00:31] Maya: Great. Goal for today is to walk through your workload shape, constraints (security/compliance), and what dedicated means for you — then we can talk about pre-warm/burst handling and next steps for a pilot.

[00:45] Samir: Cool — high level, we have two modes: the core product path that needs sub-300ms p95 for short responses and a marketing/event path where we have big bursts (big spikes) for 30-120 minutes. Baseline traffic is relatively low — maybe 40 rps during weekdays — bursts can be 200 rps for short windows. We care a lot about data isolation, and auditability — SOC2 type stuff.

[01:12] Jordan: Thanks. When you say p95 sub-300ms, is that end-to-end including network hops, or token generation time?
[01:18] Samir: It's user-perceived, so includes our network and the model. We're comfortable adding a small margin for routing, but ideally Redwood's serving time is 150-200ms p95 for the shortest generation path.

[01:30] Maya: Got it. Can you give a sense of prompt size / average token output? That matters for kernel selection and throughput.
[01:36] Nina: Average prompt is 40 tokens, response about 60 tokens; but we have heavier long-form flows that do 400 tokens occasionally. Bulk of traffic is short though.

[01:48] Jordan: That token distribution favors low-latency optimized kernels with KV cache for multi-turn. For bursts, we typically advise a prewarm/warm-pool reserved node pattern so you can absorb sudden EPS without cold-start tail latency.

[02:02] Ethan: Can you explain warm-pool vs pre-warm? We looked through the docs but the terms overlap for us.

[02:07] Jordan: Sure — 'warm-pool' in our terminology is a pool of reserved GPUs with hot model instances already loaded into memory and with KV caches pre-warmed for a known set of prompts. Pre-warm more narrowly means spinning containers or instances just before an expected spike. Warm-pool is continuous reserved capacity; pre-warm is ephemeral. Warm-pool helps with spontaneous spikes and avoids problem of disk/weight loads.

[02:33] Samir: S o in practise we'd want some reserved baseline and then a burst buffer for marketing spikes. We don't want other tenants on the same GPU as our critical workload — isolation is required.

[02:44] Maya: You can pick dedicated nodes with single-tenant assignment, we call that tenant fencing / dedicated tenancy. We also offer node-level isolation inside Dedicated, and for strictest controls we can do Private deployments in your VPC or on-prem. What's your preference for network — VPC peering, private link, or full customer-managed VPC?

[03:01] Samir: We prefer VPC peering or PrivateLink. Data residency and flow must stay within our cloud account; we need to control egress rules and enforce KMS for all key material. SOC2 is a requirement for our customers.

[03:12] Jordan: We support customer-managed VPC for Private mode. For Dedicated we can do VPC peering with encrypted links and integrate KMS for secrets and model keys. HSM-backed signing is available for on-prem/private customers.

[03:25] Nina: On auditing — we need per-request audit logs that tie tokens to route and model version. Is that native to Redwood?

[03:31] Maya: Yes, our console exposes per-route tracing, token breakdown and audit logs. For Dedicated/Private we can retain logs in your S3/audit endpoints or stream to your SIEM — retention configurable.

[03:43] Ethan: About fallback: if our reserved pool is saturated during a big burst, what's the fallback behavior — do requests fail or can they be routed to hosted instances?

[03:51] Jordan: We offer smart routing policies — you can define fallbacks: queue, reject, or route to a hosted compatible model (which may be lower-tier). For customer-critical endpoints we typically configure a canary fallback to a slightly lower-capacity model with different latency/cost characteristics. This preserves availability but changes output distribution slightly.

[04:10] Priya: How do you quantify cost tradeoffs? If we keep a large warm-pool for spikes that's expensive; if we rely on pre-warm we might have cold starts. We need to justify cost.

[04:21] Maya: Good question. Redwood Optimize recommends a hybrid: modest reserved baseline sized to handle typical peaks (e.g., 2-3x baseline) with a burst runway implemented as pre-warm + auto-burst for short windows. We can show probabilistic cost models — i.e., expected monthly reserved cost vs on-demand cost given your historical spike distribution. Jordan can run simulations if you share request histograms.

[04:44] Samir: We'll share histograms, yes. Another— how sticky is KV cache across model variants? If we fallback to a smaller quantized model during bursts, will conversations degrade badly?

[04:54] Jordan: KV cache is model-specific. If you fallback to a compatible variant (same architecture but quantized weights), we can migrate KV cache pointers if kernel layout is compatible. But full fidelity requires identical model binary; quantized variants may have subtle output drift. Part of our Optimize toolkit flags regressions and we can run eval prompt sets to quantify delta.

[05:18] Nina: What's the onboarding timeline? If we sign a reserved contract how long to provision?

[05:23] Maya: Standard provisioning for Dedicated reserved pools is usually 2-4 weeks depending on GPU availability and region. Private on-prem will be longer due to network and keys. For urgent needs we offer interim hosted capacity to avoid downtime during provisioning.

[05:36] Ethan: Can we run a pilot against our test harness? We have synthetic load generator and sample prompt set.

[05:41] Jordan: Absolutely. Jordan: We can spin up a small dedicated pool for benchmarking and run your traffic shape. Send us the payloads and we'll schedule runs — we'll measure p50/p95/p99, token cost, throughput, and memory/kv behaviors.

[05:52] Samir: Okay we'll prepare payloads. One security question — do you support SAML SSO + RBAC for model access for dedicated customers?

[05:59] Maya: Yes SAML/SSO and RBAC are supported. We can integrate with your IdP and enforce route-level permissions. Audit trails are available and immutable logs can be forwarded to your SIEM.

[06:10] Priya: Are there any listed compliance certificates we can share with our legal team?

[06:15] Maya: We have SOC 2 Type II and can provide SOC attestation. For private/on-prem deployments some attestations are customer-managed. We'll attach security docs to the follow-up email.

[06:24] Nina: Model versioning and rollouts — how do you handle canary traffic split and rollback?

[06:29] Jordan: Our Console supports canary/A-B rollouts with traffic percentages, and automatic rollback if latency or quality regressions cross thresholds. You can pin model versions per route. Also supports function/tool calling and structured outputs.

[06:40] Samir: On network egress, we need to ensure no data leaves our account — can Redwood's hosted fallback be configured to strip payloads or maintain strict residency?

[06:49] Maya: For strict residency we recommend Private deployment. For Dedicated in Redwood cloud we can configure routing to avoid using hosted fallback, or only allow fallback to your private deployment. Some customers accept fallback to a hosted curated model but we document data-flow clearly.

[07:03] Ethan: Let's talk numbers — baseline 40 rps, burst to ~200 rps for 30-120 minutes, p95 target sub-300ms, average payload 100 tokens. What reserved footprint would you recommend?

[07:16] Jordan: Rough back-of-envelope: if you need ~150 rps sustained during spike and short responses, one A100-class GPU can do N rps depending on model/quantization. For Llama-70B-like family you'll need more. I'd request the exact model family — are you using open Llama/Meta derivatives or proprietary forks?

[07:34] Samir: We're primarily on a tuned 13B family for high-throughput endpoints and 70B for occasional long-form. We'll likely run 13B in prod for majority.

[07:43] Jordan: For 13B quantized we can sustain significantly higher concurrent requests per GPU. Probable setup: baseline reserved of 2 GPUs for the 13B cluster (handle baseline + small spikes), plus 2-4 warm GPUs in a burst pool pre-loaded for marketing windows. We'll size in the benchmark.

[07:58] Priya: For contract, do you have minimum terms or ramp commitments?

[08:03] Maya: Dedicated reserved contracts typical are 12-month with monthly/annual commitments. Flex options for ramping exist; we can propose a 6-month pilot with conversion credits to full-year if you sign within the pilot window.

[08:16] Samir: That sounds reasonable. One more — how do you handle GPU preemption or maintenance? We need availability SLAs.

[08:22] Jordan: We offer SLA-backed uptime for Dedicated. We also have automated failover to a standby pool, and for critical routes we recommend multi-region placement and warm standby. Maintenance windows are scheduled with notice and we can apply live migration strategies to minimize disruption.

[08:39] Nina: Are there known limitations around persistent KV caches for long conversation sessions? We have 8-12 hour sessions in some workflows.

[08:46] Jordan: KV caches live in memory; for very long sessions we support externalized session persistence to your Redis/managed store. For our default runtime it's in-memory per model-instance and we provide APIs to snapshot or reload session state. If you need full 8-12 hour state we'd recommend a small state store to back the KV so instances can be rehydrated.

[09:04] Ethan: Regarding observability — can we get token-level cost breakdowns per route to attribute spend to product lines?

[09:10] Maya: Yes the Console provides per-route token breakdowns and per-request latency. For Dedicated we can export daily reports and push to your billing bucket.

[09:18] Samir: Anything around security scanning of model weights? We have IP concerns with third-party weights.

[09:23] Jordan: For Private/on-prem you control the weights and signing; for Dedicated we have signing and attestations and can store checksums in your KMS. If you want to bring your own models, we support BYOM with model signing and restricted access.

[09:36] Priya: OK, recap and next steps?

[09:39] Maya: Recap: Redwood recommends a pilot: small dedicated pool to benchmark your 13B traffic pattern; configure warm-pool for burst handling; integrate SAML and KMS; share SOC2 and security docs; and we will send pricing and contract.

[09:52] Samir: Action items — we'll export histograms and sample prompts, and sign NDAs as needed.

[09:58] Maya: Perfect — Jordan, you'll coordinate the benchmark and I'll send pricing and security docs.

[10:03] Jordan: Will do. I'll also include a template runbook for warm-pool bump policies and fallback gating.

[10:10] Maya: Any other questions from LatticeWave?

[10:14] Nina: Nothing else right now. Thanks.

[10:16] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with a calendar invite for the SE deep dive and the pricing.

[10:22] (meeting ends)
